summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a standalone offline web page which helps you to pick where and when to land in the vicinity of the Moon's south pole. It uses NASA's 5m LOLA terrain for six candidate sites in two of the NASA listed sites. For any site and any date it will show the real Sun and real Earth above the real horizon so a team can see when there is sunlight for power and a clear line of sight to Earth for comms. There's a calendar tool which will go through every start date for a mission of a given length, a power tab which will compare different panel layouts and a comms tab which will tell you when Earth is in view of the NASA Deep Space Network stations.

Every answer is tagged with a High, Medium or Low trust rating based on its performance across 100 different versions of the ground truth. We've also benchmarked against the published figures for Apollo 11, Chandrayaan-3 and IM-2 and in 7 of the 7 cases we're within the stated margins. The tool is of immense value to mission planners, students and educators who want to make better landing decisions using open NASA data.
details:
future Moon missions want to go to the south pole because of water ice. At our spots the Sun never goes higher than 2 degrees above the horizon so a ridge a few meters high can decide if a lander has power. The Earth. Disappears over the month because of libration so the direct radio link comes and goes. When a mission date changes planners must quickly check dates and nearby sites. NASAs expert tools are hard for people who're not specialists to use.

WHAT WE BUILT

One HTML file of 35 MB. To run it download "Lunar Landing Site Navigator.html" from our GitHub repository. Open it in Chrome, Edge or Firefox. It works without an internet connection. Needs no installation. It covers two of NASAs 27 listed south-pole sites (Site 01 Connecting Ridge and Site 04 Shackleton rim) three candidate spots each on NASA LOLA 5 m terrain with 60 m terrain out to about 95 km. Sun and Earth directions are calculated in the page with the open-source astronomy-engine library. Published libration formulas. There is no atmosphere in the model.

EIGHT TABS

- 3D view: the Sun and Earth above the real horizon with a countdown to sunset.

- Landing planner: a map of the site.

- Overview: sunlight share, Earth view, NASAs value and a trust label for each spot.

- Final answer and Calendar: the start dates that work for a stay of N days for six spots at once and the nearest passing date when a launch slips.

- Power: a first estimate of energy per day for flat fixed upright and Sun-tracking panels and a battery size (geometry only).

- Comms: hours Earth is in view while a Deep Space Network station can see the Moon (geometry only).

- Real missions: Apollo 11 Chandrayaan-3 and IM-2 as a check.

HOW IT WAS CHECKED

- NASA LOLA illumination maps: our Sun and Earth shares correlate at 0.93 and 0.98 (Site 01) and 0.97 and 0.97 (Site 04).

- NASAs 100 alternative grounds per site show how much each answer moves with ground error; this feeds the trust label.

- LROC photographs: 93.8 to 98.7 percent of the ground is lit or dark as in the photo.

- Three real landings: 7 of 7 numeric checks within the stated margins.

- NASA JPL Horizons: Sun elevation within 0.04 degrees.

- An independent audit recomputed the 2028 pass counts. Got the same numbers.

WHAT IS

Not the physics. NASAs Quickmap already shows illumination. Our contribution is accessibility: one page, plain words, a trust label built from NASAs own alternative data and power link and date-slip answers in one place. We do not claim to beat NASAs maps or tools.

HONEST LIMITS

The page draws the Earth 0.23 degrees too high (the page says so). Two sites of 27 no custom coordinates. Power and Comms are geometry only; thermal conditions are not modelled. Not yet tried with planners or teachers.
